## Part I
This part is based on the [*running*](../../../dataset/running.csv) dataset.  It is a dataset that records my running mileage by day of the week.  You'll be using the pipe operator and data manipulation functions, so make sure you load relevant packages.


1.  On average, which day of the week do I tend to run the most miles?  Calculate the average mileage for Monday, Tuesday, etc. to compare.
```{r,eval=T, message=F, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
running <- read.csv('../../../dataset/running.csv')
summary(running)
```

2. Convert the data to the following long format and store it as a separate data frame (**running.long**).  Note that your output might be sorted by Day (i.e., the first rows correspond to all the Monday data).  Print out the first 5 rows of your data.
```{r, eval=T}
running.long <- running %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = Mon:Sun, names_to = 'Day', values_to = 'Miles')

running.long %>%
  filter(Week=='8/8/16')
```


3. With the long format, calculate the average mileage for Monday, Tuesday, ect. and generate the following output.
```{r, eval=T}
running.long %>%
  group_by(Day) %>%
  summarise(average.miles=mean(Miles)) %>%
  arrange(desc(average.miles))
```

4. Print out the top 10 days when I ran the most miles (you should get the following information), using both **running** (wide format) and **running.long** (long format).   Discuss which format is easier in this case.   
```{r, eval=T}
# wide format: difficult
# maybe: manually sort through Monday to Sunday to find top 10
running %>%
  arrange(desc(Mon)) %>%
  slice(1:10)

# long format: easy
running.long %>%
  arrange(desc(Miles)) %>%
  slice(1:10)
```

5. Reproduce the following two graphs with **running.long** (which is much easier than using the wide format!).  They are essentially the same graph, but the first one is done with the base R **boxplot** function and the second one is done with **ggplot2** (with **theme\_classic**).

```{r,fig.height=4,fig.width=6,out.width="0.5\\linewidth",eval=T}
boxplot(running.long$Miles ~ running.long$Day,
        col='salmon',
        pch=16,
        xlab='Day',
        ylab='Miles')
```

```{r,fig.height=3,fig.width=5,out.width="0.5\\linewidth", eval=T}
running.long %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=Day,y=Miles)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill='salmon') +
  theme_classic()
```



## Part II
Take a look at the dataset **USArrests** in base R.  Run the following code to extract the state names and store it as a separate variable in the data frame.
```{r, echo=T}
#| code-fold: false
USArrests$state <- row.names(USArrests)
```

The following graph is generated using the **maps** package and based on the variable **UrbanPop** in the **USArrests** dataset.  Reproduce this graph (you can visualize other variables in the **USArrests** dataset instead of **UrbanPop**, if you prefer).  You can find sample code from Lecture 6 [here](../lectures/lecture_notes/index.qmd).


```{r, eval=T, message=F, warning=FALSE}
library(maps)

USArrests$state <- row.names(USArrests) %>% tolower()
mymap <- map_data(map="state")

# Combine crime data to map data
mymap <- left_join(mymap, USArrests, by=c('region'='state'))

# Visualize
mymap %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=long,y=lat,group=group, fill=UrbanPop)) +
  geom_polygon(color='darkblue') +
  coord_fixed(1.4) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(fill='Urban population percentage') +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="yellow", high="blue")
```
